summary: Monaco has no border controls of its own — entry follows Schengen rules applied through France, so EU/EEA citizens enter freely, visa-exempt nationalities get 90 days within the shared Schengen allowance, and visa-required travelers need a French-issued Schengen visa, which is valid for Monaco.

passportValidity.text: Schengen document rules apply in practice: non-EU passports should be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure and have been issued within the last 10 years. EU/EEA citizens only need a valid passport or national ID card.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000 — the French-issued visa that covers Monaco carries the standard Schengen insurance requirement. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it.

source.name: Prince's Government of Monaco — official portal

onwardTicket.text: There are no border checks between France and Monaco, so nothing is verified on the way in, but standard Schengen rules apply at the external border where you enter the area, where officers may ask about return travel.

source.name: Prince's Government of Monaco — official portal

proofOfFunds.text: No separate Monegasque check exists; France's means-of-subsistence guidelines apply to Schengen visa applicants at the external border. Visa-free visitors are rarely asked.

source.name: Prince's Government of Monaco — official portal

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders on your way to Monaco — Monaco itself has no border controls. Registration happens at the border — there is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: French and EU rules apply in practice: cash of €10,000 or more must be declared when crossing the EU external border on your way to or from Monaco.

source.name: Prince's Government of Monaco — official portal

payments.text: Cards and contactless are accepted essentially everywhere in Monaco, from cafés to the casino; cash is rarely needed.

safety.text: Monaco is one of the safest places in the world, with a very high police presence and extensive CCTV. Petty theft is rare even in crowds; the main practical concerns are traffic and event-time congestion.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Monaco Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: April–June and September–October offer warm Riviera weather without the August crush; late May is Grand Prix week, spectacular but crowded and expensive.

tips.text: There are no border checks between France and Monaco, but carry your passport anyway — hotels must record ID, and police can carry out spot checks.
Monaco is not formally a Schengen member, but you can only reach it through the Schengen Area — in practice days spent in Monaco are counted within your 90-in-180 Schengen allowance.
During the Monaco Grand Prix (late May) hotel prices multiply and much of the center is barriered off. Book far ahead, or stay in Nice and take the 20-minute train.
The Casino de Monte-Carlo has an entry fee, a dress code in the evening and an ID check — under-18s cannot enter the gaming rooms, and Monegasque citizens are not allowed to gamble.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Monaco?
faq.answer: Monaco issues no tourist visas and has no border controls. Entry is governed by Schengen rules through France. EU/EEA citizens enter freely, visa-exempt nationalities (US, UK, Japan and about 60 others) get 90 days within the Schengen allowance, and visa-required travelers need a French-issued Schengen visa, which is valid for Monaco.

faq.question: Is Monaco in the Schengen Area?
faq.answer: Not formally — Monaco is not an EU or Schengen member. But it has an open border with France and applies Schengen entry rules in practice, and French authorities handle visas and external border checks on its behalf.

faq.question: Do I need my passport for a day trip from Nice to Monaco?
faq.answer: There are no checks on the train or road from France, but you should still carry your passport or EU ID card — hotels and the casino check ID, and police can ask for documents.

faq.question: How can I stay in Monaco longer than 90 days?
faq.answer: You need a French long-stay visa (type D) applied for via France-Visas and endorsed for Monaco, followed by a residence permit (carte de séjour) application with the Monaco authorities after arrival, plus proof of accommodation and substantial means. Start with the official gouv.mc portal.

faq.question: How long can US citizens stay in Monaco?
faq.answer: Up to 90 days in any 180-day period, counted together with time spent in the Schengen Area — Monaco does not give you a separate allowance on top of your Schengen days.
